questions.q: Who can see a #local temp table?
options: Only the session that created it, plus any stored procedures that session calls
Every session connected to the server
Only the database administrator
No one — local temp tables can never be queried
questions.explain: A single # prefix scopes the temp table to just the creating session.

questions.q: Who can see a ##global temp table?
options: Every session connected to the server, not just the one that created it
Only the session that created it
Only sessions on a different physical server
No sessions — global temp tables are write-only
questions.explain: The double ## prefix makes the temp table visible across all connections to the server.

questions.q: When is a #local temp table automatically dropped?
options: When the creating session disconnects, or sooner if explicitly DROPped
Only when the entire server restarts
Never — it must always be dropped manually
As soon as any other session tries to read it
questions.explain: Local temp tables are cleaned up automatically at the end of the session that created them.

questions.q: When is a ##global temp table automatically dropped?
options: When the creating session disconnects AND no other session is still actively referencing it
Immediately after the first INSERT statement
Every night at midnight
It is never automatically dropped under any circumstances
questions.explain: Global temp tables persist a bit longer than local ones — they survive until no session is still using them.

questions.q: Why are global temp tables considered risky?
options: Any connection can read and write to them, so concurrent sessions can collide, and naming collisions across unrelated scripts are possible
They cannot store any data types other than INT
They are always slower than permanent tables
SQL Server limits a server to only one global temp table ever
questions.explain: Cross-session visibility is powerful but introduces concurrency and naming risks a permanent table or local temp table avoids.
